The Transformer architecture replaced recurrence and convolution with
self-attention as the primary mechanism for modeling sequences. Each layer
computes attention scores between every pair of tokens in the input, letting
the model weigh distant tokens just as easily as neighboring ones. This
removes the sequential bottleneck that limited recurrent networks, since all
positions can be processed in parallel during training.

A Transformer block combines multi-head self-attention with a position-wise
feed-forward network, each wrapped in a residual connection and followed by
layer normalization. Multiple attention heads let the model attend to
different representation subspaces at different positions simultaneously,
which in practice lets one head track syntactic relationships while another
tracks longer-range semantic dependencies.

Because self-attention has no inherent notion of token order, positional
encodings are added to the input embeddings before the first layer. The
original design used fixed sinusoidal functions of different frequencies,
though later variants learn the positional embeddings instead or use
relative position schemes.

The encoder-decoder split in the original architecture suited sequence-to-
sequence tasks like machine translation: the encoder builds a contextual
representation of the source sequence, and the decoder attends to both its
own previous outputs and the encoder's representation to generate the target
sequence one token at a time. Later models dropped one half or the other —
decoder-only architectures became the dominant pattern for large language
models, while encoder-only architectures became the standard for embedding
and classification tasks.

Training a Transformer at scale is largely a matter of data and compute
rather than architectural novelty, which is part of why the same core block
has powered nearly every major language model since its introduction.
